Macedon and much of mainland Greece under Cassander, son of the regent Antipater, who ruled from about 317 BCE until his death in 297 BCE. The map shows it in 300 BCE.

After Alexander the Great died, his generals fought over his empire in the Wars of the Diadochi. Cassander seized Macedon and had Alexander's mother Olympias put to death in 316 BCE. A few years later he had Alexander's widow Roxana and their young son, Alexander IV, killed, ending the royal line. He married Alexander's half-sister Thessalonike and named a new city after her, Thessalonica, still the second city of Greece. He also rebuilt Thebes, which Alexander had destroyed.

He fought Antigonus for control of Greece and joined the alliance that beat him at the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE. After Cassander's death his sons quarrelled, and by 294 BCE Demetrius, son of Antigonus, had taken Macedon. To the east lay the Kingdom of Lysimachus.
sum: Macedon and much of mainland Greece under Cassander, son of the regent Antipater, who ruled from about 317 BCE until his death in 297 BCE. The map shows it in 300 BCE.
